About: a plucked string drawn as a sum of its normal modes

Source

Concept
Normal modes of an ideal string fixed at both ends (Fermi Notes, §2.4, Fig. 26), and the motion of a string pulled aside at one point to a height yₚ and released from rest.
Serves
Fermi Notes §2.4, A String Plucked at a Point: superposition of normal modes, the wave speed v = √(τ/μ) with τ the tension and μ the mass per unit length, and the string's motion over a full period.
On screen
Two posts a length L apart, a dashed equilibrium line, and the string drawn through 801 equally spaced points as the sum of its first M normal modes, y = Σ aₙ sin(nπx/L) cos(nπvt/L), with aₙ = 2yₚL² sin(nπxₚ/L)/[n²π²xₚ(L − xₚ)]. The displacement is exaggerated: yₚ is drawn as one fifth of L. The view is fixed at 0 to L across and ±1.25yₚ up and down. The scale under the posts marks every L/8. The strip at the foot plots the mode amplitudes |aₙ|/yₚ for n = 1 to 20 on a log scale: bars for the modes summed (n ≤ M) are filled, the rest outlined, a × marks each mode with a node at xₚ, which is absent, and two dotted guides fall as 1/n² (the largest aₙ can be, 2yₚL²/[n²π²xₚ(L − xₚ)]) and as 1/n (the fall-off near a post, 2yₚL/[nπ(L − xₚ)] or 2yₚL/[nπxₚ] for the nearer post).
Controls
Time t, in units of L/v, in steps of 0.005 L/v, with chips for L/8v, L/4v, L/2v and L/v; ▶ Play advances it at 0.125 L/v per second at 1× and returns it to 0 after 2L/v. Moving the pluck point xₚ (0.10L to 0.90L) plucks the string afresh and sets the time to 0. The modes selector sets M, the number of terms summed: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 or 200.
Measured
Time read beside the time slider to 0.001 L/v; positions along the string read against the eighth-L scale; heights judged against the equilibrium line and the posts.
Inquiry
Six questions, each about the string's shape at a stated time, pluck point or number of modes summed, then a closing summary card. The chips beside the time slider jump to the exact times the questions name.
Misconception
Everyday intuitions about the shape a plucked string takes after release, tested against the drawn modal sum.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit, then checkEach of the six questions is answered before its explanation appears; the sim stays fully playable throughout.
No lookup leakThe canvas shows only the posts, the equilibrium line, the string and a fixed scale; nothing marks or names any feature of the string.
Operational quantitiesTime is read to 0.001 L/v and positions against the eighth-L scale; every number on screen is one a question names.
Stable scaleThe view is fixed and never rescaled with t, xₚ or M, so every change in the drawing is a change in the string.
Honest modelThe string drawn is always the M-term modal sum itself; the exaggeration of yₚ to one fifth of L is stated.
Formal layerThe derivation and the mode amplitudes live in The Physics sheet, apart from the scene.
A String Plucked at a Point
✦Teach me
The string between its two posts

Guided Inquiry

1 · Just after release

The string starts pulled up at xₚ = 0.25L with 200 modes summed. Set the time to t = L/8v, which the readout shows as 0.125 L/v. What shape does the string have?

2 · The far half

Move the time slider slowly from 0 to t = L/4v, which the readout shows as 0.250 L/v, watching the half of the string from L/2 to the right post. What does that half do?

3 · Back from the post

Set the time to t = L/2v, which the readout shows as 0.500 L/v. What does the string look like near the left post?

4 · One crossing, t = L/v

Set the time to t = L/v, which the readout shows as 1.000 L/v. What shape does the string have?

5 · Mode 1 alone

Keep the time at t = L/v and set the number of modes summed to 1. Where is the lowest point of the string now?

6 · Plucked at the middle

With 200 modes summed, move the pluck point to the middle of the string, xₚ = 0.50L, which sets the time back to zero, and then set the time to t = L/2v, which the readout shows as 0.500 L/v. What does the string look like?

7 · What you found

The plucked string is the sum of its normal modes, and enough modes keep the sharp corners. On release the corner splits in two; each runs at v = √(τ/μ) and comes back upside down from a post.

At t = L/v the shape is the start flipped upside down and end to end; at 2L/v, the period, it is back. Mode 1 alone is only the smooth bow.

The Physics

A String Plucked at a Point · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A string of length L is fixed at two posts, pulled aside at the point xp to a height yp and let go from rest. The sim draws it as the sum of its first M normal modes, and you move through time t in units of L/v, where v = √(τ/μ) is the wave speed.

What you'll learn

  • What the string, the scale and the mode strip show.
  • Why a string with one corner is a sum of normal modes.
  • How its shape depends on t, xp and M.
The starting shape, to the sim’s vertical exaggeration.

What's on screen

  • Blue line: the string, the sum of M modes at 801 points. The dashed line is the equilibrium line, and the grey bars are the posts.
  • Strip at the foot: |an|/yp for n = 1 to 20 on a log scale. Filled bars are modes summed (n ≤ M); a × marks an absent mode.
  • Dotted guides in the strip fall as 1/n² and 1/n.
  • Scale under the posts: a mark every L/8. Heights are exaggerated: yp is drawn as L/5.
See itStart from your current settings and press Show me. Watch for: the string, the scale and the mode strip, with the time and M in the toast.

03

The string is a sum of normal modes

Fixed at both posts, the string has normal modes sin(nπx/L), and mode n swings at ωn = nπv/L (notes 2.4). Released from rest, every bn is zero (2.71), so the motion is a sum of the modes with coefficients (2.72):

y = Σ an sin(nπx/L) cos(nπvt/L)   an = 2ypL2 sin(nπxp/L) / [n2π2xp(L − xp)]
Notes (2.71) and (2.72), the sum the sim draws.

The coefficients go as 1/n2, the rate for a shape whose slope jumps while its value does not. A mode with a node at xp is absent: at xp = L/4, n = 4, 8, 12 and so on. The strip at the foot of the sim plots |an|/yp, and the first is a1 = 0.764 yp.

xp = L/4n = 1234
an / yp0.7640.2700.0850
xp = L/4n = 5678
an / yp−0.031−0.030−0.0160
|an|/yp for the pluck at L/4, with the 1/n2 guide dotted.
See itThe sim shows the pluck at L/4 with all 200 modes. Watch for: the bars of the strip falling away, with a × at every fourth mode.
04

Released from rest, the corner splits in two

For a string released from rest, y(x, t) = ½[yi(x − vt) + yi(x + vt)], where yi is the starting shape continued as an odd function beyond each fixed end (d’Alembert; notes 2.4). Each copy is a zigzag whose corners run at v = √(τ/μ), one each way, and two straight lines add to a straight line. So the string is straight everywhere except at the two moving corners.

From xp = L/4 the corners sit at xp − vt and xp + vt. At t = L/8v they are at L/8 and 3L/8, at heights 0.50 yp and 0.83 yp, and the string is three straight segments with no corner left at L/4. Beyond the right-hand corner the string is still its starting shape, so the half from L/2 to the post does not move until t = L/4v, when that corner reaches L/2. By then the other corner is at the left post, and the string is a triangle of height 0.667 yp with its apex at L/2.

t = 0, L/8v and L/4v. The starting shape is dashed; dots mark the corners.
See itThe sim sweeps t from 0 to L/4v at xp = L/4. Watch for: the single corner becoming two, and the right-hand end of the string staying put.
05

A post turns the corner upside down

A fixed end holds y = 0, so a corner that arrives there comes back inverted, as a pulse reflects from a fixed end, and it stays sharp. The left-moving corner reaches the left post at t = L/4v. By t = L/2v it is back at xp = L/4, now below the line, at −yp/3 (the sim’s sum gives −0.332 yp).

The other corner has run on to 3L/4, still above the line at +yp/3. So at t = L/2v the string runs down from the left post to a corner at L/4, up through the line at L/2 and over a corner at 3L/4, then down to the right post.

Pluck at the middle instead and the two corners reach the posts together at t = L/2v. The string is then straight along the equilibrium line, with no slope anywhere, so the potential energy ½τ∫(∂y/∂x)2dx of (2.74) is zero and all of the energy is kinetic.

The same time, t = L/2v, for two pluck points.
See itThe sim sweeps t to L/2v at xp = L/4, then plucks at L/2 and shows the same time. Watch for: the corner returning below the line, then the string lying flat on it.
06

At t = L/v the shape is flipped over

By t = L/v each corner has crossed the whole string once and been inverted at a post. The oddness of the extension gives y(x, L/v) = −yi(L − x) (notes 2.4): the starting shape upside down and reversed end to end, as in the bottom panel of Figure 26.

The two corners meet at L − xp = 3L/4, below the line at −yp. The sum of 200 modes gives −0.997 yp there, and the lowest point of the whole string is at 3L/4.

A further L/v restores the starting shape. Every ωn = nπv/L is a whole multiple of ω1, so each term of the series repeats after 2L/v, and so does the string (2.71). The sim’s t runs from 0 to 2L/v, then starts over.

The string at t = L/v, with its starting shape dashed.
See itThe sim sweeps t from 0 to L/v at xp = L/4. Watch for: the corners travelling out, turning at the posts and meeting at 3L/4 below the line.
07

One mode cannot make a corner

A single term a1 sin(πx/L) cos(πvt/L) is a smooth bow about the middle with no corner. The corner is a jump in slope, built by the harmonics acting together with coefficients that fall as 1/n2.

At the moment of release the sum reaches yp at xp only as M grows. For xp = L/4, M = 1 gives 0.540 yp. At t = L/v one mode alone is the same bow upside down, with its lowest point at L/2, at −a1 = −0.764 yp. It never puts the corner at 3L/4. The corners need the harmonics together.

xp = L/4, t = 0M = 131050200
y(xp) / yp0.5400.8710.9510.9890.997
The sum at t = 0 for M = 1, 3, 10 and 200.
See itThe sim steps M from 1 up to 200 at t = 0 and xp = L/4. Watch for: the bow gaining a corner as modes are added, and the height at L/4 rising towards yp.
08

Where it matters

  • A guitar string plucked near the bridge. For xp ≪ L and n much below L/xp, an ≈ 2ypL/[nπ(L − xp)] falls only as 1/n, so the high harmonics are relatively stronger and the tone is brighter (notes 2.4). The sim’s nearest pluck is 0.10 L, where a2/a1 = 0.476, against 0.354 at L/4.
  • Plucked against struck. Each mode keeps the energy En it was given (2.77), since an ideal string passes none between modes. Plucked, En falls as 1/n2. A narrow hammer at the same point gives energies that do not fall until n of order L/σ, so a struck string is richer in high harmonics (2.78–2.81, Figure 27).
|an|/yp for two pluck points, n = 1 to 10.
Go deeper: the energy in the lowest modes

By (2.78), En is proportional to sin2(nπxp/L)/n2. For xp = L/4, mode 1 holds 54.0% of the energy and the first five modes 89.2%. For xp = 0.10 L, mode 1 holds only 21.5% and the first five 79.1%.

See itThe sim shows the pluck at 0.10 L, all 200 modes. Watch for: the strip falling away more slowly than at L/4, the dotted 1/n guide closer to the bars.
09

Summary

In one line. A plucked string is the sum of its normal modes: step through the time, the pluck point and the number of modes, and watch what happens to its corners.

Key points

  • Released from rest, the corner at xp splits in two; the corners run at v = √(τ/μ), and the string is straight between them.
  • A fixed end turns a corner upside down, and at t = L/v the string is flipped over and end to end.
  • The motion repeats after 2L/v. One mode makes a bow, and the harmonics make the corners.

Common mix-ups

  • “The triangle just shrinks, the corner staying at L/4.” At t = L/8v there are two corners, at L/8 and 3L/8.
  • “The corner comes back from the post the right way up.” A fixed end inverts it: at t = L/2v the string dips below the line at L/4.
  • “At t = L/v the pluck is back where it started.” That takes 2L/v. At L/v the corner is at 3L/4, below the line.

Things to try on your own

  • Pluck at L/2 and step t through L/4v and L/2v.
  • Set M = 1 and watch the string at t = L/v.
  • Compare the strip at xp = 0.10 L and 0.50 L.
